title_original: From You Can See Everything to Take That: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

Going out: Cinema

You Can See Everything Out now “Masterpiece” – it’s an overused word, but sometimes, it’s the only word. This funny, tragic, gripping, three-hour sensation (and, yes, masterpiece) arrives in the UK after a record-busting run in the States, where Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s portrait of their time immersed in the world of Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has gripped US audiences.

Josephine Out now Winner of the Audience and Grand Jury prizes at Sundance, this drama sees eight-year-old Josephine become witness to a horrific assault on a jogger in San Francisco’s Golden Gate park. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan star as the girl’s parents.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Out now Mahershala Ali stars as a former military hitman dealing with multiple crises. These range from orders to assassinate a Muslim porn studio head honcho’s charismatic Christian enemy, to finding fresh breast milk for his baby daughter, whose mother has recently passed, and who can’t digest formula.

Filipiñana Out now Seventeen-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) works at an elite golf course in the Philippines as a “tee-girl” – setting golf tees in the ground so that wealthy golfers don’t have to suffer the indignity of bending down themselves to do it. An examination of national identity as well as a personal drama, it marks the debut of director Rafael Manuel. Catherine Bray
Going out: Gigs

blocks.alt: Three members of Jungle pose closely together, two wearing sunglasses, against a clear sky
blocks.caption: Jungle, booked. Photograph: Mason

blocks.text: Jungle to 28 November; tour starts Leeds With a Brit win, a Mercury nod and five Top 10 albums, dance-pop trio Jungle have quietly (and, let’s be honest, pretty anonymously) become one of Britain’s biggest bands. Their stealthy rise is cemented via this arena tour in support of August’s Sunshine album. Michael Cragg

Knats Future Yard, Birkenhead, 21 November; Waiting Room, Stockton-on-Tees 22 November This jazz, rock and dance trio’s punky “geordie jazz” started making waves in 2025. Their latest release, A Great Day in Newcastle, reveals hard-hitting poetry, humour, and a rebellious energy sure to take them far. John Fordham

Manchester Collective Lakeside Arts, Nottingham, 25 November; touring to 6 December The latest programme from this boundary-storming contemporary music ensemble mixes an experimental work by Icelandic soundtrack queen Hildur Guðnadottir with Bach chorales and movements from James Tenney’s 1980s electroacoustic classic Glissade. At its centre lies Black Gold, Luke Mombrea’s powerfully atmospheric audiovisual piece inspired by an oil well fire. Flora Willson

Action All Areas Roundhouse, London, 26 November Self Esteem, James Bay and Jade Bird are the musical performers at this one-off night of “intimate and unplugged” music and activism in aid of Greenpeace. It’s hosted by comedian and writer Sophie Duker. MC
Going out: Art

blocks.alt: Barbara Hepworth’s wooden sculpture “Corinthos” shows curving looped forms with pale hollow interiors
blocks.caption: Barbara Hepworth, Corinthos, 1954. Photograph: Madeleine Buddo/Barbara Hepworth © Bowness/Tate

blocks.text: Barbara Hepworth and Greece Pallant House, Chichester, to 2 May Arguably Britain’s most important modernist, Barbara Hepworth found inspiration for her elegant, curving sculptural forms everywhere. But a journey through Greece in 1954 changed everything for her, and this exhibition shows us the gorgeous results. Nan Goldin Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November to 14 March Get ready to feel a lot of feelings. American photographer Nan Goldin has spent her career documenting queer subcultures, personal relationships and addiction, often to devastating effect.

Ragnar Kjartansson Goodwood Art Foundation, Chichester, 26 November to 12 April This playfully melancholic Icelandic conceptualist was last on these shores with a hugely popular Barbican show 10 years ago, and now he’s bringing his signature blend of humour and discomfort to Chichester.

Peggy Guggenheim in London Royal Academy of Art, London, to 14 March Peggy Guggenheim became one of the biggest and most important art collectors of the 20th century, and it all started on Cork Street in London. This exhibition looks at Guggenheim’s first gallery venture in 1938, and the way it shocked conservative British tastes. Eddy Frankel
Going out: Stage

blocks.alt: In The Nutcracker, two male dancers leap mid-air in splits beside a ballerina on stage
blocks.caption: Stocking thriller … Birmingham Royal Ballet’s Nutcracker. Photograph: Johan Persson

blocks.text: Birmingham Royal Ballet: The Nutcracker Birmingham Hippodrome, to 12 December One of the best Nutcrackers you’ll see in the UK, Birmingham Royal Ballet’s production was presented as a gift to the company by former director Peter Wright back in 1990 and has been a hit ever since. It ticks all the Christmas boxes: giant tree, falling (and dancing) snowflakes, and a full orchestra playing Tchaikovsky’s magical music. Lyndsey Winship

Eurotrash Young Vic, London, to 9 January A stellar double act – Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter – lead this stage adaptation of Christian Kracht’s darkly comic novel. It’s about a formidable mother and son who embark on a road trip across the Swiss mountains, intent on giving away the (slightly dodgy) family money, stashed in a plastic bag. Miriam Gillinson

My Fair Lady Pitlochry Festival theatre, to 31 December Alan Cumming stars alongside Verity Power in a chamber production of My Fair Lady, the final show of Cumming’s opening season as artistic director. It’s directed by Maria Friedman, whose work always has such grace and wit. MG

Sam Campbell Touring to 1 December Four years after winning Edinburgh’s best show prize, the Aussie eccentric has infiltrated the comedy mainstream; first as a contestant on Last One Laughing: UK, then via his surreal Channel 4 series Make That Movie. His new standup show Kid Giblet promises plenty more absurd flights of fancy. Rachel Aroesti

Staying in: Streaming

blocks.alt: Ella Purnell in character as Sweetpea, holds a shopping basket in a convenience store aisle
blocks.caption: Murder she wrote … Ella Purnell in Sweetpea. Photograph: Sky

blocks.text: Sweetpea NOW & Sky Atlantic, 26 November , 9pm Fallout’s Ella Purnell is back as the wispily fringed Rhiannon, a meek outsider who finds her niche in vigilante serial killing in this smart and gruesome drama that reflects wryly on female empowerment and the concept of embracing your flaws. Will she continue to get away with murder in series two?

The Witch Farm iPlayer & BBC One, 22 November , 9pm King of the contemporary ghost story Danny Robins has adapted his Radio 4 drama about a couple who (unintentionally) move to a haunted farm in south Wales in the late 1980s into a goosebump-inducing TV thriller. Black Doves’ Gabrielle Creevy and This Is England’s Michael Socha co-star.

Oobah: Scams For A Better Tomorrow HBO Max, 22 November Fraudsters, grifters, conmen: to be alive today is to be besieged by bad actors – and Oobah Butler wants a piece of their pie. That’s the droll setup of his new series, which will really see the prankster documentarian highlight swindles in areas including wine, wellness and dating.

Blade Runner 2099 Prime Video, 25 November This sequel to the 1982 and 2017 films picks up the action a half-century later, when lab-grown humanoids rule over LA’s actual human inhabitants. Our protagonists are replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and human-pretending-to-be-a-replicant Cora (Hunter Schafer) who team up to track down a bunch of their awol peers. RA
Staying in: Games

blocks.alt: Video game scene showing robots battling on a pinball-style arena with flippers and score numbers
blocks.caption: Flipping great… Appulse. Photograph: Le Rado/Raw Fury Games

blocks.text: Appulse PC, out 26 November An ingenious combination of pinball machine and top-down shooter, Appulse has you blasting enemy spaceships while rebounding between flippers and bumpers earning special upgrades. Surely, a veteran gamer’s dream.

Am I Nima? PC, out 27 November Locked in a basement and suffering from amnesia, you must convince your mum that you are in fact her daughter. Created by Vancouver studio Ho! Games , this is a psychological horror game with a truly interesting and unnerving premise. Keith Stuart
Staying in: Albums

blocks.alt: Kurt Wagner of Lambchop, in glasses and a cap, closes his eyes while singing
blocks.caption: A Kurt above … Lambchop. Photograph: Graham Tolbert

blocks.text: Lambchop – Demoed Out now In August Kurt Wagner shared his 17th album as Lambchop, a folk freakout titled Punching The Clown. This followup EP finds guest artists singing over a handful of that album’s demos. Vocalists include MJ Lenderman, Lauren Auder and Flock of Dimes.

Take That – Dreamers Out now Gary, Mark and Howard return with the 10th Take That album and their fourth as a trio. Eschewing the soft-rock sound of 2023’s musty This Life, songs such as the Stuart Price co-produced You’re a Superstar and the loved-up Sweet July are stadium-shaped pop stompers.

Bodywash – Laughing at Noise Out now Inspired by EVOL-era Sonic Youth and the harsh reality of city life, Montreal duo Rosie Long Decter and Chris Steward’s third album feels rougher around the edges than 2023’s shoegazey I Held the Shape While I Could. Single La Renommée carries a ragged but hushed sense of urgency.

REM – Reveal 25th Anniversary Edition Out now Hailed as a return to form in 2001 after the experimental Up, the 12th album by REM gets a 25th-anniversary rerelease. As well as the original 12-track album, led by the excellent Imitation of Life, the package features a previously unreleased 17-song live set. MC
Staying in: Brain food

blocks.alt: Willem van der Helm’s Barent Fabritius.
blocks.caption: Photograph: Rijksmuseum, via Arkivism

blocks.text: Arkivism.com Online This ingenious archive collates the collections and catalogues made available by museums and institutions around the world and presents them on one, easily searchable website. Explore paintings from Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum and images from the British Library.

World of Secrets: Dr Skin Podcast The BBC’s investigations series returns with a gripping five-part deep dive into how one of the founders of modern dermatology, Dr Albert Kligman, conducted experiments on prison inmates, often leaving them with lasting health consequences.

One Last Order Netflix, 24 November A surprisingly moving and quietly intimate film following Floridian fast-food worker Sighle Williams on her last day of service. Her bosses announce every cent earned will go to Williams and joyous community spirit ensues. Ammar Kalia
